tagline: Up the Missouri through the lands of five Sioux tribes.
intro: The Missouri leads this road nearly all the way, some 350 miles from the Chief Standing Bear Bridge on the Nebraska line north to the Cannonball River in North Dakota. It crosses the lands of the Yankton, Crow Creek, Lower Brule, Cheyenne River and Standing Rock Sioux, mostly above a river the dams have made into long lakes, Lake Sharpe behind Big Bend Dam and Lake Oahe above Pierre.

The byway sets out to tell history from the Native American point of view, and the dams are part of it. Big Bend Dam displaced people of the Crow Creek and Lower Brule reservations, and Fort Yates now stands on the shore of Lake Oahe.

moments.title: Dignity of Earth and Sky
moments.text: On a bluff over the Missouri near Chamberlain, a 50-foot stainless steel woman in Plains dress receives a star quilt whose blue diamonds move in the wind.

moments.title: Sitting Bull Monument
moments.text: Korczak Ziolkowski's bust of Sitting Bull looks over the Missouri near Mobridge, whose name is a railroad contraction of Missouri Bridge.

moments.title: Fort Yates
moments.text: Standing Rock Sioux tribal headquarters. Sitting Bull was buried here after his killing in 1890. Whether some or all of his remains went to Mobridge in 1953 is disputed. Each place has a monument.

practical: Between Eagle Butte and Mobridge the route offers a choice, gravel BIA Route 7 west of the river or Highway 83 on the east side.
